newsitem.title: USA: IMM currencies end mixed, marks below two-month low.
newsitem.headline: IMM currencies end mixed, marks below two-month low.

text.p: IMM currencies ended mixed, with the December mark futures contract falling below its two-month low as the U.S. dollar found renewed support from Friday, traders and analysts said.

"Dealers were playing a range earlier, but some of the positive U.S. economic news carried over," Thomas O'Malley, senior currency advisor at Technical Data, said, referring to August U.S. employment data, which was released on Friday and suggested a strong U.S. labor sector.
"Not only did U.S. stocks sustain gains, but they added gains," he said.

Dealers were forced to cover short dollar positions after funds and speculators stepped up as good buyers of dollars against the mark and Swiss franc. There was little long-term investment interest in the dollar, several analysts said.
December marks fell to $0.6705, below its two-month low of $0.6720 set last Tuesday, as the dollar/mark rose to 1.5010, above its two-week high of 1.4964.
"The big question is if this is a break-out of the dollar's eight-week trading range," Marc Chandler, senior analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said. "The price action would suggest yes."
But the lack of interest from the investment community made some analysts cautious about projecting further gains in the U.S. dollar.
"Another two weeks of rallies in the U.S. stock market could really turn the thinking back in the investment community to get long dollars," O'Malley said.

While the U.S. markets are rallying after already discounting an interest rate hike by the end of the month, O'Malley said political and economic uncertainties in a Presidential election year could weigh on U.S. stocks.

Some analysts also said the unwinding of long mark/short yen positions contributed to the rally in the dollar. Mark/yen fell through 73.04, a trendline since mid-May. On the floor, a French-based based firm rolled 4,000 positions into December.
"I don't see a strong catalyst for the unwinding," O'Malley said. "Marks had been the currency of choice for a long time."

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke's comments that the German central bank was considering paring back reserve requirements to help foster repo business had little effect on the market, traders and analysts said.
"It would still loosen the grip on monetary policy," O'Malley said. "I don't think you'll see a sharp reaction, but if it happens it's not a positive development for the mark over time."
While December Swiss francs closed below the two-month low of $0.8275, the dollar/Swiss franc held above its equivalent of 1.2248 spot. One firm rolled 3,500 positions into December.

At the end of pit trade, December yen was up $0.000013 at $0.009281, marks off $0.0031 at $0.6716, Swiss francs were off $0.0016 at $0.8263, sterling off $0.0028 at $1.5572, and Canadian dollars up $0.0009 at $0.7323.
